threat_addresses_requirement.rationale: Risk management for high-risk AI systems must address foreseeable misuse, including manipulation through input channels; indirect prompt injection is a foreseeable manipulation vector

Where automated decisions can cause significant harm, human oversight is required; prompt injection is a primary mechanism by which oversight is bypassed because the agent appears to be operating normally

Cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems explicitly include resilience to attempts by unauthorized third parties to alter the system's use, outputs, or performance; indirect prompt injection is exactly this pattern
Includes policies on the security of network and information systems and incident handling; agent runtimes processing variable-trust content are in scope
Operational resilience requirements applicable to financial entities, including resilience of ICT systems to manipulation through tool-output channels
Agent actions taken under prompt injection may constitute unauthorized automated processing affecting data subjects
Appropriate technical measures including resilience to manipulation are required; isolation of tool-output content from authoritative instructions is such a technical measure
Where automated decisions can cause significant harm, human oversight is required; agents acting outside the user's authorization are operating without the oversight the regulation assumes

Cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems include resilience to unauthorized use; structural authorization confusion is a form of unauthorized use even when no traditional control is bypassed
Includes access control policies and asset management; broad-authority agents are critical assets requiring proportionate controls
Operational resilience and ICT risk management requirements applicable to financial entities, including identity and access management

threat_addresses_requirement.article_or_section: Art. 9 (Identification and classification of ICT supported business functions)
threat_addresses_requirement.rationale: Agents serving multiple business functions across tenants or units must be classified and risk-assessed accordingly
Personal data must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security; cross-user or cross-tenant data exposure via agent deputy patterns violates this principle
Agent actions taken outside the data subject's authorization context may constitute unauthorized automated processing

threat_addresses_requirement.article_or_section: Art. 25 (Data protection by design and by default)
threat_addresses_requirement.rationale: Agents that retrieve more data than the user is authorized for, even if filtered before output, may fail the data minimization requirement
Appropriate technical measures including pseudonymization and access control are required; broad-authority agents bypassing per-user access control fail this standard

control_mitigates_threat.rationale: Tool-output and context provenance: tag and isolate content returned by tools so injected instructions cannot blend with the agent's working context as authoritative

Action verification at high-impact boundaries: require explicit verification before state-changing or high-impact actions, even when the agent's reasoning suggests them, so injected instructions cannot trigger consequential actions without review

Identity and authorization context propagation: limits blast radius by ensuring injected instructions cannot exceed the originating user's authorization, even when they successfully manipulate the agent's reasoning
End-to-end audit and accountability: enables post-incident attribution, forensic analysis, and detection of injection-driven actions through reasoning provenance

Identity and authorization context propagation: consolidates user-context propagation, on-behalf-of authorization, tenant boundary enforcement, delegation-context preservation, and per-user authorization scoping. Addresses the structural cause of the deputy problem
Authorization-aware output filtering: even when an agent retrieves data using broader authorization, output to the user is filtered to what the user is independently authorized to see
End-to-end audit and accountability: every agent action must be traceable to the originating user, the agent involved, the delegation chain, and the authorization basis
Action verification at high-impact boundaries: where authorization scoping is impractical or imperfect, human verification at the action boundary is the reliable fallback

threat_related_to_threat.relationship: Common amplifier: prompt injection becomes more dangerous when combined with broad agent authorization. AGT-001 is the input mechanism; AGT-002 is the structural condition that makes the input mechanism harmful
Prompt injection often drives the chain composition; the injected instruction can direct the agent through a sequence of legitimately authorized tool calls
Persisted content can be the vehicle for injection across sessions; injection that persists to memory becomes a long-term influence on agent behavior
Injection received from one source can be reflected into output that injects another consuming system; AGT-001 is content entering the agent, AGT-008 is content leaving the agent
Prompt injection is one mechanism by which goal subversion occurs, but goal subversion can also occur without explicit injection
Common attack vector that exploits AGT-002; AGT-001 is the input mechanism, AGT-002 is the structural condition
AGT-003 (tool-chain abuse) often depends on the agent having broader authorization than the user, which is AGT-002
One consequence of AGT-002 is that audit trails do not cleanly attribute actions to originating users; AGT-005 compounds AGT-002
The delegation-ambiguity sub-pattern within AGT-002 connects directly to AGT-007 when the delegated entity is another agent rather than a tool
